more of these values:
- **WHY, not WHAT** — rationale, incident, constraint the code cannot carry
- **Wider context** — where this sits architecturally; what depends on it
- **Important use cases / flows** — when to reach for it
- **Boundary contract** — dos/don'ts, valid inputs, error behavior
- **Guarantees** — thread safety, nil handling, invariants
- **Network edge** — `See docs/<feature>.md` wiring a critical point into the repo brain

**The three-test standard** — every comment (and every rung-2 doc, for test 3) must pass all three:

1. **Toolbox-value test**, two-sided:
   - *Floor (delete test):* a prose line that delivers none of the toolbox values
     is trash — cut it. Named failure modes: restated identifiers, generic filler
     ("provides validation functionality"), narrated implementation, menu sections
     filled without earning their place, **review-defense narration** — the
     writer arguing with an imagined reviewer ("bounds-checked: it never indexes
     an empty slice", "deliberately narrow — not a generalized table"); a design
     choice that needs defending is defended in the feature doc, not at the code
     line — **restated repo idiom** — a comment justifying a convention the repo
     already applies everywhere (a pointer field meaning "omitted vs explicit
     zero", the standard error-wrapping style); the convention is documented once
     at rung 2, never re-explained at each use site — and **provenance and
     decoder-ring references** — PR numbers, review items, plan/decision/test-plan
     IDs ("T-04-02", "D-07"), requirement tags ("REQ-SVC-01"), spec section refs
     ("spec §4"), "the previous behavior" narration, "matching what <old system>
     did". A decoder-ring token fails even when it resolves inside a repo doc: the
     reader gets the fact as plain prose and the doc through the one See-edge —
     never through a code they must look up. The floor's lens is the 5-year reader
     test: a reader five years out cares how the product behaves NOW, never which
     PR or review round produced it. History is rewritten as present-tense
     rationale, and an incident/ticket reference survives only when it IS the
     rationale for a constraint — never as provenance.
   - *Ceiling (smart choice):* the comment as a whole must carry the highest-value
     toolbox items for that symbol's tier within its budget. A crossroads whose
     five lines are all boundary trivia while the architectural WHY is missing
     fails, even though each line individually "adds something".
2. **Budget test** — the comment fits its tier budget (accounting and tiers below).
3. **Plain-English test (the empathy test)** — write for a fresh graduate whose
   first language may not be English: everyday words, short sentences, one idea

   the comment must be understandable BEFORE reading the code; forward references
   to other comments fail.

`See docs/<feature>.md` network-edge line (only as its own trailing line), short
inline example lines (2-4 lines).

| Tier | Role signals | Budget | Typical content |

### Comment policy (rung 1 — tiered budget)

The WHY is the default content of a doc comment, and it lives inside a hard budget:
**1–5 prose lines**, scaled to the symbol's importance. Not all symbols are born
equal — the budget forces each comment to carry only the most important facts *for
that symbol*; everything else moves up to the feature doc (rung 2), where depth is
cheap, and the `See docs/<feature>.md` edge carries the pointer.

**The Comment Value Toolbox** — a comment earns its lines by delivering one or
more of these values:
- **WHY, not WHAT** — rationale, incident, constraint the code cannot carry
- **Wider context** — where this sits architecturally; what depends on it
- **Important use cases / flows** — when to reach for it
- **Boundary contract** — dos/don'ts, valid inputs, error behavior
- **Guarantees** — thread safety, nil handling, invariants
- **Network edge** — `See docs/<feature>.md` wiring a critical point into the repo brain

**The three-test standard** — every comment (and every rung-2 doc, for test 3) must pass all three:

1. **Toolbox-value test**, two-sided:
   - *Floor (delete test):* a prose line that delivers none of the toolbox values
     is trash — cut it. Named failure modes: restated identifiers, generic filler
     ("provides validation functionality"), narrated implementation, menu sections
     filled without earning their place, **review-defense narration** — the
     writer arguing with an imagined reviewer ("bounds-checked: it never indexes
     an empty slice", "deliberately narrow — not a generalized table"); a design
     choice that needs defending is defended in the feature doc, not at the code
     line — **restated repo idiom** — a comment justifying a convention the repo
     already applies everywhere (a pointer field meaning "omitted vs explicit
     zero", the standard error-wrapping style); the convention is documented once
     at rung 2, never re-explained at each use site — and **provenance and
     decoder-ring references** — PR numbers, review items, plan/decision/test-plan
     IDs ("T-04-02", "D-07"), requirement tags ("REQ-SVC-01"), spec section refs
     ("spec §4"), "the previous behavior" narration, "matching what <old system>
     did". A decoder-ring token fails even when it resolves inside a repo doc: the
     reader gets the fact as plain prose and the doc through the one See-edge —
     never through a code they must look up. The floor's lens is the 5-year reader
     test: a reader five years out cares how the product behaves NOW, never which
     PR or review round produced it. History is rewritten as present-tense
     rationale, and an incident/ticket reference survives only when it IS the
     rationale for a constraint — never as provenance.
   - *Ceiling (smart choice):* the comment as a whole must carry the highest-value
     toolbox items for that symbol's tier within its budget. A crossroads whose
     five lines are all boundary trivia while the architectural WHY is missing
     fails, even though each line individually "adds something".
2. **Budget test** — the comment fits its tier budget (accounting and tiers below).
3. **Plain-English test (the empathy test)** — write for a fresh graduate whose
   first language may not be English: everyday words, short sentences, one idea
   per sentence. Failure modes: fancy vocabulary, stacked clauses, academic
   phrasing, unexplained acronyms/insider jargon. Second half, **self-standing**:
   the comment must be understandable BEFORE reading the code; forward references
   to other comments fail.

**Budget accounting** — prose lines count; free: blank `//` separator lines, the
`See docs/<feature>.md` network-edge line (only as its own trailing line), short
inline example lines (2-4 lines).

**Role-based tiers**:
| Tier | Role signals | Budget | Typical content |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Helper** | small method, plain constructor, obvious accessor | 0–1 prose line | one-line summary |
| **Contract** | parsing constructor, self-validating type, ordinary exported API | 2–3 prose lines | WHY + boundary contract |
| **Crossroads** | entry point, orchestrator, state machine, feature front door | up to 5 prose lines | WHY, architectural context, use cases + See-edge |

**Visibility default — unexported symbols get no comment.** Defaults to **zero**
comment lines: the name is the documentation, and a name that needs a comment wants
a rename or an extraction first. The special case is **one line carrying a very
high-value toolbox item** — a constraint or fact the code cannot carry. If a
private symbol seems to need more than that one line, the knowledge belongs to the
exported symbol that uses it, the package doc, or the feature doc.

Boundary with R3-storifying: block comments *inside* function bodies are R3's (each
is an extraction candidate, fix = a function named after the comment); doc comments
*on* exported symbols are R9's (must carry why/context, not restate the identifier).

4	
5	A real 143-line file from a JSON-RPC-over-HTTP client (anonymized), written by an
6	LLM flow before the visibility default existed. It detects which codec decoded a
7	reply body: JSON, or the client's configured non-JSON codec (msgpack). Every one
8	of its nine unexported symbols carries a comment; the file has more comment lines
9	than code lines. Each comment, judged alone, "delivers a toolbox value". The file
10	as a whole is unreadable — a human reviewer of a sibling PR called the style
11	"utterly lacking empathy for the reader".
12	
13	This is the case law for R9's visibility default: **unexported symbols get no
14	comment; the special case is one line carrying a very high-value toolbox item.**
15	
16	## The before — representative excerpts
17	
18	A 5-line comment on a private constant, with cross-repo provenance:
19	
20	```go
21	// nonJSONLeadingByteFloor is the lowest leading byte a non-JSON wire
22	// frame can start with in the leading-byte detection heuristic:
23	// JSON-RPC 2.0 envelopes always start with '{' (0x7b), and msgpack maps
24	// (fixmap, map16, map32) always start at 0x80 or above — the same
25	// boundary the legacy client's detectCodec uses.
26	nonJSONLeadingByteFloor byte = 0x80
27	```
28	
29	Decoder rings and review-defense narration on another constant:
30	
31	```go
32	// msgpackAliasContentType is the second literal spelling D-04 requires
33	// this package to accept as msgpack, alongside jsonrpc.ContentTypeMsgpack
34	// ("application/msgpack"). Named as a single constant — not a table —
35	// per Pitfall 3: a third wire format would earn its own narrow check,
36	// not a generalized alias registry.
37	msgpackAliasContentType = "application/x-msgpack"
38	```
39	
40	Six lines on a one-line function, with forward references to its callers:
41	
42	```go
43	// trimUTF8BOM strips a leading UTF-8 BOM from data, returning data unchanged
44	// when no BOM is present. Used both to classify a reply's byte verdict
45	// (detectReplyCodec) and, for a JSON verdict, to decode it
46	// (Client.ParseResponse): encoding/json treats a BOM as an invalid leading
47	// byte rather than whitespace, so leaving it in would still fail to decode
48	// even after correct classification.
49	func trimUTF8BOM(data []byte) []byte {
50	    return bytes.TrimPrefix(data, utf8BOM)
51	}
52	```
53	
54	A caller list that rots on the next caller:
55	
56	```go
57	// normalizeContentType strips any ";"-delimited parameters (e.g.
58	// "; charset=binary"), trims surrounding whitespace, and lowercases the
59	// result — the shared normalization step both isMsgpackAliasContentType and
60	// replyCodecAndMismatch's header cross-check use (see codec_event.go).
61	func normalizeContentType(headerContentType string) string {

65	budget of an exported crossroads — ending in a sixty-word sentence:

68	// replyCodecAndMismatch returns the byte-verdict codec (identical to
69	// detectReplyCodec) plus a bool that is true when the normalized
70	// Content-Type header disagrees with that byte verdict. The byte verdict
71	// always governs the actual decode (D-04: bytes-first); mismatch is only a
72	// signal for the caller's CodecEvent, never a second decode selector.
73	//
74	// headerSaysNonJSON is true when the header exactly names nonJSON's own
75	// content type, OR — the msgpack-alias carve-out D-04 requires — the
76	// header is either msgpack spelling AND nonJSON's content type IS msgpack
77	// (the alias never claims agreement for an unrelated non-JSON codec).
78	//
79	// An empty body never mismatches: it is not a valid non-JSON envelope
80	// regardless of what the header claims.
81	//
82	// A Client with no distinct non-JSON codec configured (nonJSON is the
83	// jsonrpc.JSONCodec{} default) never mismatches either: with nothing but
84	// JSON to disagree with, an ordinary JSON reply's own "Content-Type:
85	// application/json" header would otherwise satisfy headerSaysNonJSON's
86	// literal string comparison against nonJSON.ContentType() (also
87	// "application/json"), producing a false-positive mismatch on every
88	// zero-config JSON call — a bug this guard forecloses rather than lets a
89	// caller's mismatch check ever observe.
90	func replyCodecAndMismatch(data []byte, nonJSON jsonrpc.Codec, headerContentType string) (jsonrpc.Codec, bool) {
91	```

94	
95	All nine symbols are unexported, so the question is existence, not size:
96	
97	| Symbol | Before | Verdict | Why |
98	|---|---|---|---|
99	| `nonJSONLeadingByteFloor` | 5 lines | one-liner survives | the WHY of the magic number ('{' is 0x7b; msgpack maps start at 0x80) — the code cannot carry it |
100	| `msgpackAliasContentType` | 5 lines | DELETE | the name and value say it; "D-04 requires" is a decoder ring; "not a table, per Pitfall 3" is review-defense narration |
101	| `utf8BOM` | 6 lines | one-liner survives | an ordering constraint: 0xEF ≥ the floor, so the BOM check must run before the leading-byte check |

106	| `isMsgpackAliasContentType` | 5 lines | DELETE | the name says it; decoder rings and review-defense again |

108

110	
111	## The after
112	
113	```go
114	package jrpchttp
115	
116	import (
117	    "bytes"
118	    "strings"
119	
120	    "example.com/rpc/jsonrpc"
121	)
122	
123	const (
124	    // JSON envelopes start with '{' (0x7b); msgpack maps start at 0x80 or above.
125	    nonJSONLeadingByteFloor byte = 0x80
126	
127	    msgpackAliasContentType = "application/x-msgpack"
128	)
129	
130	// A BOM's lead byte (0xEF) is above the floor, so strip it before the leading-byte check.
131	var utf8BOM = []byte{0xEF, 0xBB, 0xBF}
132	
133	func trimUTF8BOM(data []byte) []byte {
134	    return bytes.TrimPrefix(data, utf8BOM)
135	}
136	
137	func detectReplyCodec(data []byte, nonJSON jsonrpc.Codec) jsonrpc.Codec {
138	    data = trimUTF8BOM(data)
139	    if len(data) == 0 {
140	        return jsonrpc.JSONCodec{}
141	    }
142	    if data[0] >= nonJSONLeadingByteFloor {
143	        return nonJSON
144	    }
145	
146	    return jsonrpc.JSONCodec{}
147	}
148	
149	// encoding/json treats a leading BOM as an invalid byte, not whitespace, so JSON strips it.
150	func replyBytesForDecode(codec jsonrpc.Codec, rawResponse []byte) []byte {
151	    if _, isJSON := codec.(jsonrpc.JSONCodec); isJSON {
152	        return trimUTF8BOM(rawResponse)
153	    }
154	
155	    return rawResponse
156	}
157	
158	func normalizeContentType(headerContentType string) string {
159	    contentType := headerContentType
160	    if idx := strings.IndexByte(contentType, ';'); idx >= 0 {
161	        contentType = contentType[:idx]
162	    }
163	
164	    return strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(contentType))
165	}
166	
167	func isMsgpackAliasContentType(headerContentType string) bool {
168	    switch normalizeContentType(headerContentType) {
169	    case string(jsonrpc.ContentTypeMsgpack), msgpackAliasContentType:
170	        return true
171	    default:
172	        return false
173	    }
174	}
175	
176	// The body bytes always pick the decoder; a disagreeing Content-Type header is only reported, never trusted.
177	func replyCodecAndMismatch(data []byte, nonJSON jsonrpc.Codec, headerContentType string) (jsonrpc.Codec, bool) {
178	    codec := detectReplyCodec(data, nonJSON)
179	    if len(data) == 0 || nonJSON.ContentType() == jsonrpc.ContentTypeJSON {
180	        return codec, false
181	    }
182	
183	    headerSaysNonJSON := normalizeContentType(
184	        headerContentType,
185	    ) == normalizeContentType(
186	        string(nonJSON.ContentType()),
187	    ) ||
188	        (isMsgpackAliasContentType(headerContentType) && nonJSON.ContentType() == jsonrpc.ContentTypeMsgpack)
189	    bodySaysNonJSON := codec.ContentType() != jsonrpc.ContentTypeJSON
190	
191	    return codec, headerSaysNonJSON != bodySaysNonJSON
192	}
193	```

198	The exported API (`Client.ParseResponse`, the mismatch event) is where a reader
199	meets this package; that is where the tier budgets and the See-edge live.

204	decides whether it should exist at all. Before this case, "Helper: 0–1 lines"

209	special case is **one line carrying a very high-value toolbox item** — an
210	ordering constraint, an external library quirk, the WHY of a magic number, the
211	package's one real policy. If a private symbol seems to need more than that one
212	line, the knowledge belongs to the exported symbol that uses it, the package

# R7 — Test Placement

## Principle

Every behavior is tested at the lowest rung of the composition ladder that contains
it: rung 0 is pure leaf types (unit tests with literal inputs, 100% coverage, public
API only, `pkg_test` package); each rung above adds exactly one real production
layer; only the true external boundary is ever faked.

## Why

A behavior tested above its lowest rung pays for machinery the behavior doesn't
need: big-object construction, harnesses, fakes. A conditional inside `t.Run` means
one case is really two.

## Canonical example

### Before — anti-patterns stacked
```go
package user // same package — can reach privates
func TestValidateEmailInternal(t *testing.T) { ... } // testing a private
func TestCreateUser(t *testing.T) {
    mockRepo := &MockRepository{}
    mockRepo.On("Save", mock.Anything).Return(nil)
    svc := &UserService{Repo: mockRepo}
    ...
}
func TestAsyncOperation(t *testing.T) {
    go doAsyncWork()
    time.Sleep(100 * time.Millisecond) // flaky
    ...
}
```

### After — right rung, real collaborators, observable behavior
```go
package user_test
func TestService_CreateUser(t *testing.T) {
    repo := user.NewInMemoryRepository()
    ...
}
```

## Design guidance

- Leaf types (rung 0): 100% unit coverage; `pkg_test` package.
- Orchestrating types: integration-style tests wiring real collaborators.
- Fake only the true external boundary.
- Complexity 1 inside every `t.Run`: no if/else, no switch. `wantErr bool` is the
  canonical violation.
- The urge to test a private is a placement signal, never a license.
- Mechanics: named struct fields; no `time.Sleep`.

## Fix pattern
- Move the behavior down a rung.
- Split `wantErr` tables.
- Replace doubles with real collaborators.
- Replace sleep with synchronization.
- Delete private-function tests.

## Falsifying questions

Answer each with evidence (`file:line`, command output) — never a bare verdict.

1. **Does any `t.Run` body contain a conditional?**
   Detection: `grep -rn -A6 't.Run(' --include='*_test.go' . | grep -nE 'if |switch '`
   and `grep -rn 'wantErr' --include='*_test.go' .`
   Violation: any conditional inside a case, or a `wantErr bool` field.

2. **Is any test in the internal package?**
   Detection: `grep -rn '^package ' --include='*_test.go' . | grep -v '_test$'`
   Violation: a test package without the `_test` suffix.

3. **Does a test construct a big object to exercise a leaf behavior?**
   Detection: read each test — compare setup vs. the assertion's subject.
   Violation: heavyweight construction whose assertions target logic a leaf type
   owns (or should own).

4. **Does a new behavior's test sit above the lowest rung that contains it?**
   Detection: for each new public method on a leaf type, is it exercised directly,
   or only through an orchestrator's test?
   Violation: leaf behavior reached only from above.

5. **Does a test assert on a fake's internals rather than observable behavior?**
   Detection: `grep -rn 'AssertExpectations\|AssertCalled\|\.calls\b' --include='*_test.go' .`
   Violation: the test verifies the double.

6. **Does any test sleep to synchronize?**
   Detection: `grep -rn 'time.Sleep' --include='*_test.go' .`
   Violation: any hit.

# R10 — Concurrency Safety

## Principle

Every goroutine has an owner and a provable exit path; shared mutable state is owned
by one type and guarded where it lives; production code never sleeps to pace or
synchronize cancellable work.

## Why

A leaked goroutine accumulates silently. An unsynchronized concurrent map write is a
fatal runtime crash. A bare `time.Sleep` in a retry loop holds a cancelled request
hostage for the full backoff.

## Canonical example

### Before — unowned goroutine, no exit path
```go
func StartWorker(workChan <-chan Work) {
    go func() {
        for {
            work := <-workChan
            process(work)
        }
    }()
}
```

### After — owned, cancellable, joinable
```go
type Worker struct { done chan struct{} }
func StartWorker(ctx context.Context, workChan <-chan Work) *Worker {
    w := &Worker{done: make(chan struct{})}
    go func() {
        defer close(w.done)
        for {
            select {
            case work, ok := <-workChan:
                if !ok { return }
                process(work)
            case <-ctx.Done():
                return
            }
        }
    }()
    return w
}
func (w *Worker) Wait() { <-w.done }
```

### Second case — uncancellable backoff + unguarded shared write
```go
// ❌ Before
for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
    resp, err := http.Post(...)
    if err != nil {
        time.Sleep(time.Duration(attempt+1) * time.Second) // cancelled caller waits anyway
        continue
    }
    GlobalRegistry[name] = version // fatal crash if two Deploys race
}
// ✅ After — backoff selects on ctx; state owned by one guarded type
for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
    resp, err := d.post(ctx, raw)
    if err != nil {
        if err := sleepCtx(ctx, backoff(attempt)); err != nil { return err }
        continue
    }
    d.registry.Record(name, version)
}
```

## Design guidance

- Whoever starts a goroutine owns its shutdown.
- Every blocking loop selects on its exit.
- State and its guard are one unit: mutex declared directly above the fields it
  guards, every access through that type's methods.
- Prefer handing off to sharing.
- Pick the right guard (atomic, sync.Map only for append-only/disjoint-key caches).
- Production code does not sleep.

## Fix pattern
- Inject the Exit Path.
- Make the Goroutine Joinable.
- Extract Synchronized Owner.
- Replace Sleep with Timer Select.
- Delete Unearned Guards.

2. **Can the code that starts a goroutine also stop it and wait for it?**
   Detection: for each `go` site, check what the spawning function returns/exposes.
   Violation: fire-and-forget in library code.

3. **Is shared mutable state written from a goroutine without a guard?**

   Violation: any write reachable from two goroutines with no mutex/channel

# R9 — Repo Brain (Documentation Network)

## Principle

Documentation is a network ranked by the documentation ladder: storified code →
godoc comments → repo docs → the index, each fact placed at the lowest rung that can
carry it, higher rungs summarizing and pointing down, never duplicating. Two
invariants hold the network together: reachability (every doc is reachable from
the root) and bidirectionality (code points up at its feature doc; docs point down
at code via greppable symbols; the index points everywhere).

## Comment policy (rung 1 — tiered budget)

The WHY is the default content of a doc comment, 1–5 prose lines, scaled to the
symbol's importance.

The Comment Value Toolbox: WHY not WHAT; wider context; important use cases; boundary
contract; guarantees; network edge (`See docs/<feature>.md`).

The three-test standard:
1. Toolbox-value test (floor: delete trash; ceiling: carry the highest-value items).
   Named failure modes: restated identifiers, generic filler, narrated
   implementation, review-defense narration ("bounds-checked: it never indexes an
   empty slice"), restated repo idiom, provenance/decoder-ring references (PR
   numbers, "T-04-02", "spec §4.2", "the previous behavior").
2. Budget test — fits its tier budget.
3. Plain-English test (self-standing, no jargon, no forward references to other
   comments).

Role-based tiers: Helper (0-1 line), Contract (2-3 lines: parsing constructors,
self-validating types, ordinary exported API), Crossroads (up to 5 lines: entry
points, orchestrators, state machines).

Visibility default — unexported symbols get NO comment (zero prose lines) unless one
line carries a very high-value toolbox item (ordering requirement, external library
quirk, WHY of a magic number, the package's one real policy).

## Falsifying questions

Answer each with evidence (`file:line`, command output) — never a bare verdict.
Determine the doc root first (discovery order: .ai/ → .ainav/ → docs/).

# R11 — Conditional Dispatch (Anti-IF)

## Principle

A conditional that asks what a value *is* — a type switch, or a switch/if-chain on a
kind/status/mode discriminator — may exist **once**. The second copy of that
discriminator is a missing polymorphic type.

## Why

Every `if (new kind) { new code }` doubles the execution paths. Kind-switches
replicate: the same `switch msg.Channel` appears in send, validate, format, and retry
code, and adding a variant means finding and editing every copy.

## Canonical example
A notifier delivers alerts over email, Slack, or PagerDuty via a string field,
inspected in three places (send, validate, retry) — three owners of one decision,
already inconsistent. After: `ParseChannel` is the ONLY place the raw string is
inspected; a `Channel` interface replaces the three switches.

## Design guidance

- The trigger is duplication, not existence. One site — keep the switch (make it
  exhaustive). Two or more — the variants are a type family; dispatch.
- Decide once, at the edge.
- Dispatch requires owning the output.
- Interface vs strategy map.
- Null object over nil-checks.
- Flag arguments are two functions: `func Render(a Alert, short bool)` forces every
  caller through a conditional the callee then unpicks. Split into `Render` and
  `RenderShort`.
- A kept switch must be exhaustive.
- The over-abstraction trap, dispatch edition: an interface with one production
  implementation is R6's territory; two trivial implementations behind one switch at
  one site score LOW on R1's juiciness scorecard — keep the conditional.

## Fix pattern
- Replace Duplicated Switch with Interface Dispatch.
- Replace If-Chain with Strategy Map.
- Introduce Null Object.
- Split Flag Argument.
- Keep the Single Exhaustive Switch.

## Falsifying questions

Answer each with evidence (`file:line`, command output) — never a bare verdict.

1. **Is the same discriminator inspected in more than one place?**
   Detection: list discriminators —

# R12 — Mutation Discipline (Encapsulated State)

## Principle

A validated value changes state only through methods that own its invariants — never
through leaked internals. Constructors copy the slices and maps they are given;
queries return copies (or iterators), not the internal reference; a method is a query
or a modifier, not both; and a type with a validating constructor exposes no setter
that skips the validation.

## Why

`return g.perms` does not return the permissions; it returns a mutable alias into
them. A constructor that stores a caller's slice without copying has handed its state
to code it has never met.

## Canonical example

```go
// ❌ returns a mutable alias into the validated state
func (g Grants) All() []Permission { return g.perms }
// ❌ a distant caller, months later
perms := user.Grants.All()
sort.Slice(perms, func(i, j int) bool { ... }) // reorders internal state
perms[0] = PermissionNone // corrupts it
```

```go
// ✅ All returns a copy; callers may do anything with it.
func (g Grants) All() []Permission { return slices.Clone(g.perms) }
```

Backward version: a constructor storing the caller's slice directly instead of
cloning it — later caller-side mutation of the original slice silently changes the
stored value too.

## Design guidance

- Copy at both edges: constructor clones slice/map args; query returns clone or
  iterator.
- Iterators beat copies for read paths.
- A method is a query or a modifier (Fowler: Separate Query from Modifier).
- No setters around a validating constructor.
- One variable, one purpose (Fowler: Split Variable).
- The inverse trap: ceremony copies — don't clone data that never escapes.

## Fix pattern
- Copy on the Way In.
- Copy on the Way Out / Encapsulate Collection.
- Separate Query from Modifier.
- Remove Setting Method.
- Split Variable.

## Falsifying questions

Answer each with evidence (`file:line`, command output) — never a bare verdict.

1. **Does a method return an internal slice or map by reference?**
   Detection: for each type with a validating constructor, list its slice/map
   fields, then `grep -nE 'return [a-z][a-zA-Z]*\.(<field1>|<field2>)$' <file>` — a
   bare `return x.field` with no `Clone`/copy/iterator around it.
   Violation: an internal reference escapes a validated type.

2. **Does a constructor store a caller-provided slice/map without copying?**
   Detection: inside each `ParseX`/`NewX`, check the struct literal for a slice/map
   field assigned directly from a parameter identifier.
   Violation: the type's state aliases memory the caller still holds.

3. **Does one method both return domain data and mutate the receiver?**
   Detection: for each changed method with a non-error return value, grep its body
   for assignments to receiver fields (`<recv>.<field> =`, `append(<recv>.`).
   Violation: a query/modifier hybrid where any call site discards the return
   value or calls it only for the effect.

4. **Can a validated type be mutated around its constructor?**
   Detection: `grep -rnE 'func \([a-z][a-zA-Z]* \*?[A-Z][a-zA-Z]*\) Set[A-Z]' <files>`
   Violation: a setter that assigns unchecked on a constructor-validated type.

5. **Is one variable reassigned to mean something different?**

Payload 1 — R9's Comment policy section (verbatim):

### Comment policy (rung 1 — tiered budget)

The WHY is the default content of a doc comment, and it lives inside a hard budget:
**1–5 prose lines**, scaled to the symbol's importance. Not all symbols are born
equal — the budget forces each comment to carry only the most important facts *for
that symbol*; everything else moves up to the feature doc (rung 2), where depth is
cheap, and the `See docs/<feature>.md` edge carries the pointer.

**The Comment Value Toolbox** — a comment earns its lines by delivering one or
more of these values:
- **WHY, not WHAT** — rationale, incident, constraint the code cannot carry
- **Wider context** — where this sits architecturally; what depends on it
- **Important use cases / flows** — when to reach for it
- **Boundary contract** — dos/don'ts, valid inputs, error behavior
- **Guarantees** — thread safety, nil handling, invariants
- **Network edge** — `See docs/<feature>.md` wiring a critical point into the repo brain

**The three-test standard** — every comment (and every rung-2 doc, for test 3) must pass all three:

1. **Toolbox-value test**, two-sided:
   - *Floor (delete test):* a prose line that delivers none of the toolbox values
     is trash — cut it. Named failure modes: restated identifiers, generic filler
     ("provides validation functionality"), narrated implementation, menu sections
     filled without earning their place, **review-defense narration** — the
     writer arguing with an imagined reviewer ("bounds-checked: it never indexes
     an empty slice", "deliberately narrow — not a generalized table"); a design
     choice that needs defending is defended in the feature doc, not at the code
     line — **restated repo idiom** — a comment justifying a convention the repo
     already applies everywhere (a pointer field meaning "omitted vs explicit
     zero", the standard error-wrapping style); the convention is documented once
     at rung 2, never re-explained at each use site — and **provenance and
     decoder-ring references** — PR numbers, review items, plan/decision/test-plan
     IDs ("T-04-02", "D-07"), requirement tags ("REQ-SVC-01"), spec section refs
     ("spec §4"), "the previous behavior" narration, "matching what <old system>
     did". A decoder-ring token fails even when it resolves inside a repo doc: the
     reader gets the fact as plain prose and the doc through the one See-edge —
     never through a code they must look up. The floor's lens is the 5-year reader
     test: a reader five years out cares how the product behaves NOW, never which
     PR or review round produced it. History is rewritten as present-tense
     rationale, and an incident/ticket reference survives only when it IS the
     rationale for a constraint — never as provenance.
   - *Ceiling (smart choice):* the comment as a whole must carry the highest-value
     toolbox items for that symbol's tier within its budget. A crossroads whose
     five lines are all boundary trivia while the architectural WHY is missing
     fails, even though each line individually "adds something".
2. **Budget test** — the comment fits its tier budget (accounting and tiers below).
3. **Plain-English test (the empathy test)** — write for a fresh graduate whose
   first language may not be English: everyday words, short sentences, one idea
   per sentence. Failure modes: fancy vocabulary, stacked clauses, academic
   phrasing, unexplained acronyms/insider jargon. Second half, **self-standing**:
   the comment must be understandable BEFORE reading the code; forward references
   to other comments fail.

**Budget accounting** — prose lines count; free: blank `//` separator lines, the
`See docs/<feature>.md` network-edge line (only as its own trailing line), short
inline example lines (2-4 lines).

**Role-based tiers**:
| Tier | Role signals | Budget | Typical content |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Helper** | small method, plain constructor, obvious accessor | 0–1 prose line | one-line summary |
| **Contract** | parsing constructor, self-validating type, ordinary exported API | 2–3 prose lines | WHY + boundary contract |
| **Crossroads** | entry point, orchestrator, state machine, feature front door | up to 5 prose lines | WHY, architectural context, use cases + See-edge |

comment lines: the name is the documentation, and a name that needs a comment wants
a rename or an extraction first. The special case is **one line carrying a very
high-value toolbox item** — a constraint or fact the code cannot carry. If a

exported symbol that uses it, the package doc, or the feature doc.

**Precondition check:** `models.Device` has no validating constructor at all — no `NewDevice`/`ParseDevice` anywhere in the repo (confirmed via `grep -rn 'func New\|func Parse' internal/models`, only `ParsePriority`, `NewGrants`, `ParseRegion`, `ParseTenant`, `NewSchedule` exist for other types). Every `Device` is built via bare struct literals (`internal/services/device_service.go:159,338`). So `device.go:17` `func (d *Device) SetStatus(s string)` cannot be convicted under Q4 ("setter that skips validation on a constructor-validated type") — there is no validating constructor to bypass, and `SetStatus` is never even called within the diff scope. ---

**Finding 1 — Tags slice built locally, stored into cache unfloned, and the very same backing array handed back to the caller**

`rule` | `internal/services/device_service.go:159,196,215,219` | Q2: inside `ProcessHeartbeat`, `d = models.Device{..., Tags: tags, ...}` (line 159) and later `d.Tags = tags` (line 196) assign the locally-built `tags []string` directly — no `slices.Clone`. That `d` is then written into internal state at line 215 `s.cache[tenant+"/"+id] = d`. Q1 (return path): the exact same slice is then handed to the external caller via the named return at line 219 `return id, n, changed, tags, nil`. Evidence: `id, score, changed, tags, err := svc.ProcessHeartbeat(...)` in `internal/handlers/heartbeat.go:38` receives that slice unchanged and JSON-encodes it (`heartbeat.go:43-46`) — today harmless, but the cached `Device.Tags` and the handler's `tags` are one backing array; any future call site that sorts/mutates/truncates in place (`sort.Strings(tags)`, `tags[0] = "x"`) silently corrupts the cached device without touching `s.cache` directly. | Fix pattern: **Copy on the Way In** (clone `tags` before assigning to `d.Tags`) + **Copy on the Way Out** (clone before the `return ..., tags, nil`). | S

**Finding 2 — `Get` returns the cached `Device` (and its `Tags` slice) without cloning, aliasing internal cache state**

`rule` | `internal/services/device_service.go:226,234` | Q1: `d, ok := s.cache[key]` (226) then bare `return d, nil` (234). The top-level `Device` struct is copied out of the map, but its `Tags []string` field is a slice header — copying the struct does not copy the backing array, so the returned `Device.Tags` still aliases the same memory as the cached entry's `Tags`. A caller doing `dev, _ := svc.Get(ctx, t, id); dev.Tags[0] = "x"` mutates the cache entry silently, with no lock held and no `Save` call. | Fix pattern: **Copy on the Way Out** (`d.Tags = slices.Clone(d.Tags)` before returning). | S

`rule` | `internal/services/device_service.go:371-386` (`"tags": d.Tags,` at line 377) | Q1: `Export` builds `out := map[string]interface{}{..., "tags": d.Tags, ...}` — no clone. **Finding 4 — `n` reassigned to mean three different concepts (Split Variable)**

`rule` | `internal/services/device_service.go:194,199,201-207` | Q5: `n = len(tags)` (194, tag count) → `n = n * 10 // score weight` (199, weighted partial) → `n += 100` / `n += 50` / `n = 0` (201-207, final status-adjusted score, which is then returned as the function's `n int` result at line 219 and used by the caller as `Score`, see `heartbeat.go:17,38,46`). # R4 — Helper Visibility & Placement

## Principle

Every extraction raises a second question: where does the helper live? The answer is
decided by two axes — juiciness (the scorecard in `R1-primitive-obsession.md`; cite
it, never re-derive it) and scope (feature-specific versus domain-generic). Three
rungs: unexported in place, feature sub-package, shared domain package. Never test
privates, and never export a helper into its parent package just so a test can reach
it.

## Why

Wrong placement rots in both directions. Helpers exported into the parent package for
testability pollute its API. Juicy helpers buried as unexported code either go
untested or push the team into testing privates. Role-named dumping grounds (`util`,
`helpers`, `common`) accrete unrelated code that nobody can find, name, or own.

## Canonical example

From the Port case. After extraction, `Port`/`Ports`/`FirstNamed`/`First` say nothing
about Kubernetes or Weka: juicy and domain-generic → rung 3, `internal/pkg/networking`.
The feature keeps a four-line storified policy method.

The rung-1 contrast — a trivial helper that stays put:

```go
// Trivial: one caller, no domain vocabulary, no rules of its own.
// Stays unexported; covered through the parent's public API.
func parseK3SArgument(arg string) (key, value string, ok bool) {
    parts := strings.SplitN(arg, "=", 2)
    if len(parts) != 2 {
        return "", "", false
    }
    return parts[0], parts[1], true
}
```

## Design guidance

### The placement ladder

1. **Trivial helper** → unexported, same package, tested only through the parent's
   public API.
2. **Juicy + feature-scoped** → vertical-slice feature sub-package *if the feature has
   enough substance to be a package*; types exported there.
3. **Juicy + domain-generic** → shared domain-named library package:
   `internal/pkg/<domain>` (default) or `pkg/<domain>` (public). Granularity: a
   package is a domain *vocabulary* (`networking`), not a single noun (`kubeport`),
   never a role (`util`/`helpers`/`common`).

### The promotion signal

**The urge to unit-test a helper directly means it deserves its own package.**

### The reuse objection

"Nobody else uses it, so it can't justify a package." Wrong premise: reuse is not the
only justification for extraction.

### Granularity

Name shared packages after a domain vocabulary with room for siblings.

## Fix pattern

- **Demote (rung 1)**: unexport, delete direct tests, cover through parent's API.
- **Promote to feature sub-package (rung 2)**.
- **Promote to domain package (rung 3)**.
- **Split policy from vocabulary during promotion**.
- **Move Method to the Envied Type** (Fowler: Feature Envy → Move Function): a
  function that reads another type's data more than its own belongs on that type.
- **A message chain is a placement signal, not a wrapper order** (Fowler: Message
  Chains).
- **A type speaks for its parts only when it has something to add** (Fowler: Middle
  Man).

## Falsifying questions

Answer each with evidence (`file:line`, command output) — never a bare verdict.

1. **Is a symbol exported only so tests can reach it?**
   Detection: for each newly exported func/type,
   `grep -rn '<Symbol>' --include='*.go' . | grep -v _test.go` — count non-test
   references outside its defining file.
   Violation: zero production call sites outside the package while `*_test.go`
   references exist.

2. **Are unexported helpers tested directly?**
   Detection: `grep -rL '^package .*_test$' --include='*_test.go' .` to find
   internal test packages, then grep those files for calls to lowercase functions
   defined in the package.
   Violation: any direct test of a private helper.

3. **Does a new shared package have a role name?**
   Detection: `ls internal/pkg pkg 2>/dev/null | grep -iE '^(util|utils|helpers|helper|common|shared|misc)$'`
   Violation: any hit.

4. **Is a new shared package a single noun rather than a vocabulary?**
   Detection: `grep -c '^type [A-Z]' internal/pkg/<name>/*.go`
   Violation: a package named after its one type with no room for siblings.

5. **Did feature policy leak into a shared package?**
   Detection: grep the shared package for feature-owned literals and constants.
   Violation: any feature-specific literal or preference decision inside a
   domain-generic package.

6. **Does a changed function envy another type's data?**
   Detection: for each changed function/method, count field/method accesses per
   value (receiver vs its most-touched parameter/field).
   Violation: accesses on one foreign value outnumber accesses on the receiver and
   the foreign type is yours to extend.

Payload 1 — R9's Comment policy section (verbatim):

### Comment policy (rung 1 — tiered budget)

The WHY is the default content of a doc comment, and it lives inside a hard budget:
**1–5 prose lines**, scaled to the symbol's importance. Not all symbols are born
equal — the budget forces each comment to carry only the most important facts *for
that symbol*; everything else moves up to the feature doc (rung 2), where depth is
cheap, and the `See docs/<feature>.md` edge carries the pointer.

**The Comment Value Toolbox** — a comment earns its lines by delivering one or
more of these values:
- **WHY, not WHAT** — rationale, incident, constraint the code cannot carry
- **Wider context** — where this sits architecturally; what depends on it
- **Important use cases / flows** — when to reach for it
- **Boundary contract** — dos/don'ts, valid inputs, error behavior
- **Guarantees** — thread safety, nil handling, invariants
- **Network edge** — `See docs/<feature>.md` wiring a critical point into the repo brain

**The three-test standard** — every comment (and every rung-2 doc, for test 3) must pass all three:

1. **Toolbox-value test**, two-sided:
   - *Floor (delete test):* a prose line that delivers none of the toolbox values
     is trash — cut it. Named failure modes: restated identifiers, generic filler
     ("provides validation functionality"), narrated implementation, menu sections
     filled without earning their place, **review-defense narration** — the
     writer arguing with an imagined reviewer ("bounds-checked: it never indexes
     an empty slice", "deliberately narrow — not a generalized table"); a design
     choice that needs defending is defended in the feature doc, not at the code
     line — **restated repo idiom** — a comment justifying a convention the repo
     already applies everywhere (a pointer field meaning "omitted vs explicit
     zero", the standard error-wrapping style); the convention is documented once
     at rung 2, never re-explained at each use site — and **provenance and
     decoder-ring references** — PR numbers, review items, plan/decision/test-plan
     IDs ("T-04-02", "D-07"), requirement tags ("REQ-SVC-01"), spec section refs
     ("spec §4"), "the previous behavior" narration, "matching what <old system>
     did". A decoder-ring token fails even when it resolves inside a repo doc: the
     reader gets the fact as plain prose and the doc through the one See-edge —
     never through a code they must look up. The floor's lens is the 5-year reader
     test: a reader five years out cares how the product behaves NOW, never which
     PR or review round produced it. History is rewritten as present-tense
     rationale, and an incident/ticket reference survives only when it IS the
     rationale for a constraint — never as provenance.
   - *Ceiling (smart choice):* the comment as a whole must carry the highest-value
     toolbox items for that symbol's tier within its budget. A crossroads whose
     five lines are all boundary trivia while the architectural WHY is missing
     fails, even though each line individually "adds something".
2. **Budget test** — the comment fits its tier budget (accounting and tiers below).
3. **Plain-English test (the empathy test)** — write for a fresh graduate whose
   first language may not be English: everyday words, short sentences, one idea
   per sentence. Failure modes: fancy vocabulary, stacked clauses, academic
   phrasing, unexplained acronyms/insider jargon. Second half, **self-standing**:
   the comment must be understandable BEFORE reading the code; forward references
   to other comments fail.

**Budget accounting** — prose lines count; free: blank `//` separator lines, the
`See docs/<feature>.md` network-edge line (only as its own trailing line), short
inline example lines (2-4 lines).

**Role-based tiers**:
| Tier | Role signals | Budget | Typical content |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Helper** | small method, plain constructor, obvious accessor | 0–1 prose line | one-line summary |
| **Contract** | parsing constructor, self-validating type, ordinary exported API | 2–3 prose lines | WHY + boundary contract |
| **Crossroads** | entry point, orchestrator, state machine, feature front door | up to 5 prose lines | WHY, architectural context, use cases + See-edge |

**Visibility default — unexported symbols get no comment.** Defaults to **zero**
comment lines: the name is the documentation, and a name that needs a comment wants
a rename or an extraction first. The special case is **one line carrying a very
high-value toolbox item** — a constraint or fact the code cannot carry. If a
private symbol seems to need more than that one line, the knowledge belongs to the
exported symbol that uses it, the package doc, or the feature doc.

1	# Over-Abstraction Case: The CIDRPresence Wrapper
2	
3	Demonstrates: R1
4	
5	A real refactoring where an extraction was tried, rejected, and replaced with two
6	cheaper alternatives. This is the case law for R1's over-abstraction trap: what a
7	correct refutation of a proposed type looks like.
8	
9	## The setting
10	
11	During the refactor of a K3s configuration function (`alignCIDRArgs`, originally 60
12	lines mixing string parsing, boolean flag tracking, and triplicated switch cases),
13	two booleans tracked related state:
14	
15	```go
16	var (
17	    isClusterCIDRSet bool
18	    isServerCIDRSet  bool
19	)
20	// ... a parsing loop sets them ...
21	if isClusterCIDRSet && isServerCIDRSet {
22	    return // both set, nothing to do
23	}
24	```
25	
26	Grouping them into a `CIDRConfig` domain type was a clear win (related data that
27	travels together, a query method that reads like English). The trap appeared one
28	step further: the temptation to wrap each boolean in its own type.
29	
30	## The extraction that was tried
31	
32	```go
33	// CIDRPresence — a wrapper that adds NO value
34	type CIDRPresence bool
35	
36	const (
37	    cidrPresent CIDRPresence = true
38	)
39	
40	func (p CIDRPresence) IsSet() bool {
41	    return bool(p) // just unwraps the bool!
42	}
43	
44	type CIDRConfig struct {
45	    ClusterCIDR CIDRPresence // wrapped bool
46	    ServiceCIDR CIDRPresence // wrapped bool
47	}
48	
49	func (c CIDRConfig) AreBothSet() bool {
50	    return c.ClusterCIDR.IsSet() && c.ServiceCIDR.IsSet()
51	}
52	```
53	
54	## Why it was rejected
55	
56	1. **8 lines of code** for a trivial wrapper.
57	2. **One method** that just unwraps: `return bool(p)`.
58	3. **No type safety gained** — still just a bool underneath; nothing invalid is made
59	   unrepresentable.
60	4. **Not more readable.** Compare `config.ClusterCIDR.IsSet()` (wrapper) with
61	   `config.ClusterCIDRSet` (good naming). The honest question — is the method call
62	   *significantly* clearer? — answers itself: no.
63	5. **No validation, no logic, no invariants** — pure ceremony. On R1's scorecard this
64	   scores 0-1: LOW priority, do not create the type.
65	6. **Increases cognitive load** — one more type to understand, for nothing.
66	
67	The rejection also identified the *real* need hiding under the proposal: **controlled
68	mutation**. Only the parsing code should be able to set these flags — and the wrapper
69	type does not deliver that (its fields were still freely settable). Naming the actual
70	need is what makes the cheaper alternatives findable.
71	
72	## Cheaper alternative 1 — better naming
73	
74	When the need is only clarity, rename and stop:
75	
76	```go
77	type CIDRConfig struct {
78	    ClusterCIDRSet bool
79	    ServiceCIDRSet bool
80	}
81	```
82	
83	`config.ClusterCIDRSet` reads exactly as well as `config.ClusterCIDR.IsSet()`, at
84	zero ceremony. Acceptable when mutation discipline isn't a concern (small, disciplined
85	surface; short-lived value).
86	
87	## Cheaper alternative 2 — private fields + accessors (chosen)
88	
89	When the need is controlled mutation rather than validation or logic, private fields
90	with read-only accessors deliver compiler-enforced safety without a wrapper:
91	
92	```go
93	// CIDRConfig — which CIDR configurations are present.
94	// Private fields: can only be set by ParseCIDRConfig.
95	type CIDRConfig struct {
96	    clusterCIDRSet bool
97	    serviceCIDRSet bool
98	}
99	
100	func (c CIDRConfig) ClusterCIDRSet() bool { return c.clusterCIDRSet }
101	func (c CIDRConfig) ServiceCIDRSet() bool { return c.serviceCIDRSet }
102	
103	func (c CIDRConfig) AreBothSet() bool {
104	    return c.clusterCIDRSet && c.serviceCIDRSet
105	}
106	```
107	
108	Why this beat the wrapper:
109	
110	- **Same safety** — the compiler enforces that only the parser (in the same package)
111	  can set the values; external code gets read-only access.
112	- **4 fewer lines** than the `CIDRPresence` approach.
113	- **Same readability** — `ClusterCIDRSet()` is just as clear as `ClusterCIDR.IsSet()`.
114	- **No wrapper ceremony** — the fields are what they are: bools.
115	
116	## The decision, tabulated
117	
118	| Approach | Types | Readability | Safety | Ceremony | Verdict |
119	|----------|-------|-------------|--------|----------|---------|
120	| `CIDRPresence` wrapper | 6 | Good | Low | High | ❌ Over-abstraction |
121	| Public bool fields (naming) | 5 | Good | Low | Low | ⚠️ Acceptable for disciplined scope |
122	| Private bools + accessors | 5 | Good | **High** | Low | ✅ Chosen |
123	
124	## The decision questions
125	
126	Before creating a wrapper type, ask:
127	
128	1. Does it have >1 meaningful method with logic — not just unwrapping?
129	2. Does it enforce invariants or validation?
130	3. Is the need actually *controlled mutation*? → private fields + accessors, not a
131	   wrapper.
132	4. Is the method call **significantly** clearer than good naming?
133	5. Does it hide complex implementation?
134	
135	Mostly NO → use primitives with good naming, or private fields when mutation must be
136	controlled. (Score it with R1's scorecard; this wrapper scores 0.)
137	
138	## The skeptic's operating rule
139	
140	**A refutation must always propose the cheaper alternative — never just "no".**
141	
142	Rejecting `CIDRPresence` was legitimate only because the rejection came with a design
143	that met the real need (controlled mutation) at lower cost. A bare "don't create the
144	type" would have left the original defect — uncontrolled mutation of the flags — in
145	place. The skeptic's job is therefore two moves, always together: name the need the
146	proposal was groping toward, then meet it more cheaply — better naming when the need
147	is clarity, private fields + accessors when the need is controlled mutation, and a
148	real type (per R1) only when the need is validation or behavior.

# Over-Abstraction Case: The CIDRPresence Wrapper

Demonstrates: R1

A real refactoring where an extraction was tried, rejected, and replaced with two
cheaper alternatives. This is the case law for R1's over-abstraction trap: what a
correct refutation of a proposed type looks like.

## The setting

During the refactor of a K3s configuration function (`alignCIDRArgs`, originally 60
lines mixing string parsing, boolean flag tracking, and triplicated switch cases),
two booleans tracked related state:

```go
var (
    isClusterCIDRSet bool
    isServerCIDRSet  bool
)
// ... a parsing loop sets them ...
if isClusterCIDRSet && isServerCIDRSet {
    return // both set, nothing to do
}
```

Grouping them into a `CIDRConfig` domain type was a clear win (related data that
travels together, a query method that reads like English). The trap appeared one
step further: the temptation to wrap each boolean in its own type.

## The extraction that was tried

```go
// CIDRPresence — a wrapper that adds NO value
type CIDRPresence bool

const (
    cidrPresent CIDRPresence = true
)

func (p CIDRPresence) IsSet() bool {
    return bool(p) // just unwraps the bool!
}

type CIDRConfig struct {
    ClusterCIDR CIDRPresence // wrapped bool
    ServiceCIDR CIDRPresence // wrapped bool
}

func (c CIDRConfig) AreBothSet() bool {
    return c.ClusterCIDR.IsSet() && c.ServiceCIDR.IsSet()
}
```

## Why it was rejected

1. **8 lines of code** for a trivial wrapper.
2. **One method** that just unwraps: `return bool(p)`.
3. **No type safety gained** — still just a bool underneath; nothing invalid is made
   unrepresentable.
4. **Not more readable.** Compare `config.ClusterCIDR.IsSet()` (wrapper) with
   `config.ClusterCIDRSet` (good naming). The honest question — is the method call
   *significantly* clearer? — answers itself: no.
5. **No validation, no logic, no invariants** — pure ceremony. On R1's scorecard this
   scores 0-1: LOW priority, do not create the type.
6. **Increases cognitive load** — one more type to understand, for nothing.

The rejection also identified the *real* need hiding under the proposal: **controlled
mutation**. Only the parsing code should be able to set these flags — and the wrapper
type does not deliver that (its fields were still freely settable). Naming the actual
need is what makes the cheaper alternatives findable.

## Cheaper alternative 1 — better naming

When the need is only clarity, rename and stop:

```go
type CIDRConfig struct {
    ClusterCIDRSet bool
    ServiceCIDRSet bool
}
```

`config.ClusterCIDRSet` reads exactly as well as `config.ClusterCIDR.IsSet()`, at
zero ceremony. Acceptable when mutation discipline isn't a concern (small, disciplined
surface; short-lived value).

## Cheaper alternative 2 — private fields + accessors (chosen)

When the need is controlled mutation rather than validation or logic, private fields
with read-only accessors deliver compiler-enforced safety without a wrapper:

```go
// CIDRConfig — which CIDR configurations are present.
// Private fields: can only be set by ParseCIDRConfig.
type CIDRConfig struct {
    clusterCIDRSet bool
    serviceCIDRSet bool
}

func (c CIDRConfig) ClusterCIDRSet() bool { return c.clusterCIDRSet }
func (c CIDRConfig) ServiceCIDRSet() bool { return c.serviceCIDRSet }

func (c CIDRConfig) AreBothSet() bool {
    return c.clusterCIDRSet && c.serviceCIDRSet
}
```

Why this beat the wrapper:

- **Same safety** — the compiler enforces that only the parser (in the same package)
  can set the values; external code gets read-only access.
- **4 fewer lines** than the `CIDRPresence` approach.
- **Same readability** — `ClusterCIDRSet()` is just as clear as `ClusterCIDR.IsSet()`.
- **No wrapper ceremony** — the fields are what they are: bools.

## The decision, tabulated

| Approach | Types | Readability | Safety | Ceremony | Verdict |
|----------|-------|-------------|--------|----------|---------|
| `CIDRPresence` wrapper | 6 | Good | Low | High | ❌ Over-abstraction |
| Public bool fields (naming) | 5 | Good | Low | Low | ⚠️ Acceptable for disciplined scope |
| Private bools + accessors | 5 | Good | **High** | Low | ✅ Chosen |

## The decision questions

Before creating a wrapper type, ask:

1. Does it have >1 meaningful method with logic — not just unwrapping?
2. Does it enforce invariants or validation?
3. Is the need actually *controlled mutation*? → private fields + accessors, not a
   wrapper.
4. Is the method call **significantly** clearer than good naming?
5. Does it hide complex implementation?

Mostly NO → use primitives with good naming, or private fields when mutation must be
controlled. (Score it with R1's scorecard; this wrapper scores 0.)

## The skeptic's operating rule

**A refutation must always propose the cheaper alternative — never just "no".**

Rejecting `CIDRPresence` was legitimate only because the rejection came with a design
that met the real need (controlled mutation) at lower cost. A bare "don't create the
type" would have left the original defect — uncontrolled mutation of the flags — in
place. The skeptic's job is therefore two moves, always together: name the need the
proposal was groping toward, then meet it more cheaply — better naming when the need
is clarity, private fields + accessors when the need is controlled mutation, and a
real type (per R1) only when the need is validation or behavior.

1	# Anti-IF Dispatch Case: One Decision, One Owner
2	
3	Demonstrates: R11 (edges into R1, R2, R6)
4	
5	A worked study of the R11 moves on a realistic alert-notification slice: a string
6	discriminator inspected in three files becomes an interface chosen once at the
7	boundary; a single-function variance becomes a strategy map instead; and the inverse
8	case — where the skeptic kills the extraction and the switch *stays* — is worked to
9	its cheaper alternative. The compact excerpt lives in
10	`../rules/R11-conditional-dispatch.md`; this file is the full case law.
11	
12	## The disease: a decision with three owners
13	
14	The alert feature delivers over email, Slack, or PagerDuty. `Alert.Channel` is a raw
15	string (already an R1 smell), and three sites ask what it is:
16	
17	```go
18	// ❌ alert/send.go
19	func Send(a Alert) error {
20	    switch a.Channel {
21	    case "email":
22	        return smtpSend(a.Recipient, renderEmail(a))
23	    case "slack":
24	        return slackPost(a.Recipient, renderSlack(a))
25	    case "pagerduty":
26	        return pdCreateIncident(a.Recipient, a.Summary)
27	    default:
28	        return fmt.Errorf("unknown channel %q", a.Channel)
29	    }
30	}
31	
32	// ❌ alert/validate.go — drifted: pagerduty was never added here
33	func validRecipient(a Alert) bool {
34	    switch a.Channel {
35	    case "email":
36	        return strings.Contains(a.Recipient, "@")
37	    case "slack":
38	        return strings.HasPrefix(a.Recipient, "#")
39	    }
40	    return false
41	}
42	
43	// ❌ alert/retry.go — the same decision wearing an if-chain
44	func retryDelay(a Alert) time.Duration {
45	    if a.Channel == "pagerduty" {
46	        return 0
47	    }
48	    if a.Channel == "slack" {
49	        return 5 * time.Second
50	    }
51	    return time.Minute
52	}
53	```
54	
55	Why this is a defect and not a style choice:
56	
57	- **The drift already happened.** `validRecipient` returns `false` for `"pagerduty"`
58	  — not by decision, but because the second copy of the switch was not in view when
59	  the third channel landed. Duplicated discriminators drift the same way duplicated
60	  validation predicates drift (R1's Q2).
61	- **Adding SMS is a scavenger hunt.** Three known sites, plus whatever a grep misses
62	  (test helpers, a metrics label formatter). The compiler flags none of them: an
63	  if-chain has no completeness, and a switch with a `default` swallows the new case
64	  silently.
65	- **"Unknown channel" leaks everywhere.** Every switching site carries the
66	  `default:`/fall-through arm, so every function's signature and tests carry the
67	  maybe-unknown concept — the behavioral twin of R1's maybe-invalid port.
68	- **Nothing unit-tests in isolation.** Slack's recipient rule is only reachable by
69	  driving `validRecipient` with a fully built `Alert`.
70	
71	## Move 1 — Replace Duplicated Switch with Interface Dispatch
72	
73	Define the interface from the union of what the copies do: `Send` switches on
74	delivery, `validRecipient` on addressing, `retryDelay` on retry policy — three
75	methods, one type per variant:
76	
77	```go
78	// alert/channel.go
79	type Channel interface {
80	    Send(a Alert) error
81	    ValidRecipient(recipient string) bool
82	    RetryDelay() time.Duration
83	}
84	
85	// ParseChannel is the single decision point. This switch is ALLOWED —
86	// it is the one place the raw string may be inspected (R11), exactly as
87	// a ParseX constructor is the one place a raw value is validated (R2).
88	func ParseChannel(name string) (Channel, error) {
89	    switch name {
90	    case "email":
91	        return Email{}, nil
92	    case "slack":
93	        return Slack{}, nil
94	    case "pagerduty":
95	        return PagerDuty{}, nil
96	    default:
97	        return nil, fmt.Errorf("unknown channel %q", name)
98	    }
99	}
100	```
101	
102	```go
103	// alert/slack.go — each variant is a leaf type owning ALL its behavior
104	type Slack struct{}
105	
106	func (Slack) Send(a Alert) error           { return slackPost(a.Recipient, renderSlack(a)) }
107	func (Slack) ValidRecipient(r string) bool { return strings.HasPrefix(r, "#") }
108	func (Slack) RetryDelay() time.Duration    { return 5 * time.Second }
109	```
110	
111	`Alert` now holds a `Channel`, constructed at the boundary (the HTTP handler or
112	config loader calls `ParseChannel` and fails fast there). The three switching sites
113	collapse to method calls:
114	
115	```go
116	func Send(a Alert) error            { return a.Channel.Send(a) }
117	func validRecipient(a Alert) bool   { return a.Channel.ValidRecipient(a.Recipient) }
118	func retryDelay(a Alert) time.Duration { return a.Channel.RetryDelay() }
119	```
120	
121	(And once they are one-liners, the wrappers themselves usually dissolve into their
122	callers — the story functions call the methods directly, R3.)
123	
124	What was deleted, not relocated: every `default:` arm downstream. An `Alert` that
125	exists holds a `Channel` that exists; "unknown channel" is unrepresentable past
126	`ParseChannel`. Adding SMS is now one new file (`sms.go`) plus one `case` in
127	`ParseChannel` — no existing file changes.
128	
129	**R6 check, answered explicitly:** this interface is *earned* — it has three
130	production implementations on day one. R6 forbids interfaces whose only second
131	implementer is a test double; a dispatch interface born with one variant "for the
132	future" fails that test and should stay a switch until the second variant is real.
133	
134	### The testing payoff
135	
136	Each variant unit-tests as a leaf with literals — no `Alert` construction, no
137	switch-driving:
138	
139	```go
140	func TestSlack_ValidRecipient(t *testing.T) {
141	    assert.True(t, alert.Slack{}.ValidRecipient("#oncall"))
142	    assert.False(t, alert.Slack{}.ValidRecipient("oncall"))
143	}
144	
145	func TestParseChannel_Unknown(t *testing.T) {
146	    _, err := alert.ParseChannel("carrier-pigeon")
147	    require.Error(t, err)
148	}
149	```
150	
151	The drift bug (`pagerduty` missing from `validRecipient`) can no longer be written:
152	there is no second place to forget.
153	
154	## Move 2 — Replace If-Chain with Strategy Map
155	
156	Not every variance deserves an interface. Suppose only *rendering* varies by an
157	output format, in one behavioral dimension:
158	
159	```go
160	// ❌ before: if-chain in the middle of business logic
161	func render(a Alert, format string) string {
162	    if format == "json" {
163	        return renderJSON(a)
164	    }
165	    if format == "text" {
166	        return renderText(a)
167	    }
168	    return renderMarkdown(a) // silent default — is "yaml" markdown? nobody decided
169	}
170	```
171	
172	One behavior → a map, not three types:
173	
174	```go
175	type Format string
176	
177	const (
178	    FormatJSON     Format = "json"
179	    FormatText     Format = "text"
180	    FormatMarkdown Format = "markdown"
181	)
182	
183	var renderers = map[Format]func(Alert) string{
184	    FormatJSON:     renderJSON,
185	    FormatText:     renderText,
186	    FormatMarkdown: renderMarkdown,
187	}
188	
189	func ParseFormat(raw string) (Format, error) {
190	    if _, ok := renderers[Format(raw)]; !ok {
191	        return "", fmt.Errorf("unknown format %q", raw)
192	    }
193	    return Format(raw), nil
194	}
195	
196	func render(a Alert, f Format) string { return renderers[f](a) }
197	```
198	
199	The lookup *is* the dispatch; the comma-ok check lives once, in `ParseFormat`, at the
200	boundary. The silent markdown default — an undecided decision — became an explicit
201	error. (The map is package-level immutable data, the sanctioned shape under R8;
202	naming the enum is R1's "Name enum strings" move.)
203	
204	## Move 3 — the rejection: when the switch stays
205	
206	The skeptic's side of R11, worked honestly. The same codebase has this:
207	
208	```go
209	// alert/severity.go — the ONLY site that inspects Severity
210	func (s Severity) Color() string {
211	    switch s {
212	    case SeverityInfo:
213	        return "blue"
214	    case SeverityWarning:
215	        return "yellow"
216	    case SeverityCritical:
217	        return "red"
218	    }
219	    return ""
220	}
221	```
222	
223	A dispatch-happy reading says: three variants, extract `type Severity interface`
224	with `Info`, `Warning`, `Critical` types. Score it before moving (R1 scorecard, via
225	the over-abstraction skeptic):
226	
227	- Duplication of the discriminator: **1 site** (grep `switch .*Severity` → one hit) — +0
228	- Behavioral variance: one method, returns a constant string — trivial — +0
229	- Would the interface be earned (R6)? Three implementations, but each is an empty
230	  struct wrapping one literal — ceremony
231	
232	Verdict: **REFUTED.** The extraction would turn 12 readable lines into three files
233	and an interface for zero deletion — no duplicated switch exists to delete. The
234	cheaper alternative is R11's sanctioned form, **Keep the Single Exhaustive Switch**:
235	
236	```go
237	func (s Severity) Color() string {
238	    switch s { // exhaustive: linter fails the build when a Severity is added unhandled
239	    case SeverityInfo:
240	        return "blue"
241	    case SeverityWarning:
242	        return "yellow"
243	    case SeverityCritical:
244	        return "red"
245	    }
246	    return ""
247	}
248	```
249	
250	with `exhaustive` enabled in `.golangci.yaml`. Now the linter provides what dispatch
251	would have: adding `SeverityFatal` fails the build at this switch instead of falling
252	through to `""`. That is the whole benefit, at none of the cost.
253	
254	**The dividing line, restated:** dispatch is bought with the *deletion of duplicated
255	decisions*. Three sites collapsed to one boundary — clear win (Move 1). One
256	single-dimension variance — a map (Move 2). One site, trivial variance — the switch
257	stays, made exhaustive (Move 3). If nothing gets deleted, the abstraction is
258	ceremony.
259

# Switch-to-Polymorphism Case: The Ever-Growing Export Switch

Demonstrates: R11, R6 (edges into R3)

Adapted from production code. `../examples/anti-if-dispatch.md` works R11's canonical
disease — a *raw* discriminator (a kind string) inspected at three sites. This case
is the type-switch sibling: a value that is **already polymorphic** (an interface,
dispatched once at construction) gets *un-dispatched* by a type switch that unpacks
its fields. The decision was made when the value was built; the switch asks it again.

Two things make this case worth its own file. First, the *obvious* refactoring
(extract each case body into a helper) is a trap — it shrinks the function but
preserves the disease. Second, the rejection axis here is different from
`anti-if-dispatch.md`'s Move 3: there the skeptic kills an extraction on juiciness
(one site, trivial variance); here the counter is **dependency direction** — a
situation where the dispatch move is physically unavailable and the switch is the
honest answer.

## Before — the hump that grows forever

`Patch` is an interface with one method (`Type()`) and four concrete
implementations, one per export destination. The converter interrogates each
concrete type and shovels its fields into a flat wire request:

```go
func fromUpdateArg(arg UpdateArg) updateExportRequest {
    req := updateExportRequest{Name: arg.Name}
    req.Type = arg.Patch.Type().String()

    switch p := arg.Patch.(type) {
    case SplunkPatch:
        if p.Token != nil {
            s := string(*p.Token)
            req.Token = &s
        }
    case S3Patch:
        req.S3Bucket = p.Bucket
        req.S3Key = p.Key
        req.S3Region = p.Region
        if p.Secret != nil {
            s := string(*p.Secret)
            req.S3Secret = &s
        }
    case KafkaPatch:
        req.KafkaTopic = p.Topic
        req.KafkaUseSASL = p.UseSASL
        req.KafkaSASLUsername = p.Username
        req.KafkaKeyField = p.KeyField
        if p.Mechanism != nil {
            m := p.Mechanism.String()
            req.KafkaSASLMechanism = &m
        }
        if p.Password != nil {
            s := string(*p.Password)
            req.KafkaSASLPassword = &s
        }
    case SyslogPatch:
        if p.Mode != nil {
            m := p.Mode.String()
            req.SyslogMode = &m
        }
        if p.RFC != nil {
            r := p.RFC.String()
            req.SyslogRFC = &r
        }
        if p.Facility != nil {
            f := p.Facility.String()
            req.SyslogFacility = &f
        }
    }

    req.setTLS(arg.TLS.Expand())
    return req
}
```

Three defects, and only one of them is size:

- **The decision is asked twice (R11).** Whoever constructed `UpdateArg` already
  chose `KafkaPatch` — the value is an interface *because* that decision was made.
  The type switch re-asks it. A type switch over an interface the same package owns
  is always a second ask; "decide once at the edge" was violated the moment the
  cases appeared.
- **Ask-and-unpack.** The knowledge of *how a Splunk patch serializes* lives in the
  consumer, not on `SplunkPatch`. Each variant's wire mapping has no owner.
- **Silent growth failure.** Adding a `PubSubPatch` and forgetting this switch
  compiles clean and ships a request carrying only `Name` and `Type` — a runtime
  no-op with no compiler, linter, or test to catch it unless someone remembers to
  write one. (Mixed in, an R3 note: the business flow — identity → payload → TLS —
  is buried under nil-deref-convert plumbing repeated nine times.)

## The tempting wrong fix — extract each case body

The reflexive move is Extract Function per case:

```go
case KafkaPatch:
    fillKafka(&req, p)
case SyslogPatch:
    fillSyslog(&req, p)
```

The function gets shorter and each case reads better — and nothing real changed.
The switch still exists, still grows a case per destination forever, and a
forgotten case is still a silent no-op. This is the ceiling of function
extraction, not the fix.

The falsifying question that breaks the frame: **why are we switching on type and
extracting data at all?** A type switch whose cases all do the same *kind* of work
(map my fields onto that struct) is behavior asking to live on the types. The
cased types already share an interface — the switch is a hand-rolled vtable.

## After — the interface owns the behavior

Add the fill behavior to the interface the concrete types already implement:

```go
// Patch is implemented by each export-destination patch type.
// fillUpdate writes the destination-specific fields onto the wire request;
// shared fields (Name, Type, TLS) belong to the caller.
type Patch interface {
    Type() ExportType
    fillUpdate(req *updateExportRequest)
}
```

The orchestrator collapses to a three-beat story (R3): identity, payload, TLS.

```go
func fromUpdateArg(arg UpdateArg) updateExportRequest {
    req := updateExportRequest{
        Name: arg.Name,
        Type: arg.Patch.Type().String(),
    }
    arg.Patch.fillUpdate(&req)
    req.setTLS(arg.TLS.Expand())
    return req
}
```

Each destination owns its own mapping, in its own file (`splunk.go`, `s3.go`,
`kafka.go`, `syslog.go`):

```go
func (p SplunkPatch) fillUpdate(req *updateExportRequest) {
    req.Token = optSecret(p.Token)
}

func (p S3Patch) fillUpdate(req *updateExportRequest) {
    req.S3Bucket = p.Bucket
    req.S3Key = p.Key
    req.S3Region = p.Region
    req.S3Secret = optSecret(p.Secret)
}

func (p KafkaPatch) fillUpdate(req *updateExportRequest) {
    req.KafkaTopic = p.Topic
    req.KafkaUseSASL = p.UseSASL
    req.KafkaSASLUsername = p.Username
    req.KafkaKeyField = p.KeyField
    req.KafkaSASLMechanism = optStringer(p.Mechanism)
    req.KafkaSASLPassword = optSecret(p.Password)
}

func (p SyslogPatch) fillUpdate(req *updateExportRequest) {
    req.SyslogMode = optStringer(p.Mode)
    req.SyslogRFC = optStringer(p.RFC)
    req.SyslogFacility = optStringer(p.Facility)
}
```

Two tiny helpers kill the repeated nil-deref-convert dance that padded every case:

```go
// optStringer converts an optional enum to its optional wire-string form.
func optStringer[T fmt.Stringer](v *T) *string {
    if v == nil {
        return nil
    }
    s := (*v).String()
    return &s
}

// optSecret unwraps an optional Secret for the wire request.
func optSecret(s *Secret) *string {
    if s == nil {
        return nil
    }
    v := string(*s)
    return &v
}
```

An insert path is the same move: `fillInsert(req *insertExportRequest)` on the same
interface, and `fromInsertArg` becomes the same three-beat story.

## The payoffs

1. **Compile-time enforcement replaces a silent no-op.** A new `PubSubPatch`
   without `fillUpdate` no longer builds. The growth failure mode moved from
   "runtime request missing its payload" to "compiler error at the moment of
   authorship" — the strongest possible catch point. (This is R11's exhaustiveness
   payoff without the `exhaustive` linter: interface satisfaction *is* the
   completeness proof.)
2. **Adding a destination is a new file, not an edit.** `fromUpdateArg` is frozen
   at three beats; the switch version grows a hump per destination forever.
3. **The story survives (R3).** The orchestrator states *what* happens; each
   destination's *how* lives one level down, on the type that owns the data.
4. **The interface is earned, and sealed.** Four production implementations — this
   passes R6's earned-interface test (contrast: an interface whose only second
   implementer is a test double). The unexported method is a bonus: no code outside
   the package can implement `Patch`, so the implementation set is closed and the
   compiler-enforcement guarantee in payoff 1 cannot be bypassed.

## Fill, don't construct

Note the method signature: `fillUpdate(req *updateExportRequest)`, not
`ToUpdateRequest() updateExportRequest`. The request carries fields the patch does
not own — `Name`, `Type`, TLS come from the surrounding argument. A constructor
method would either return a partial request the caller must merge (field-by-field
merging re-creates the original mess) or need the rest of the argument passed in
(the patch learns about its container). Filling keeps ownership honest: the caller
owns the shared fields, each patch owns its own.

## The boundary counter — when the switch must stay

This move has one precondition: **the package that owns the case types must also
legitimately own the output format.** Here both `Patch` and `updateExportRequest`
live in one package (a client whose API surface and wire format are the same
concern), so the method is natural.

When the patch types live in a shared API package and the wire request is one
consumer's private detail, the move is unavailable and wrong:

- Physically: an interface method cannot reference another package's unexported
  type, and exporting the wire type just to enable the method inverts the
  dependency.
- Architecturally: with multiple consumers (CLI, gateway, store), per-consumer
  `fill<X>Request` methods accrete every consumer's serialization onto the domain
  types — interface pollution from the opposite direction.

In that situation the type switch at the consumer's boundary is idiomatic Go — the
honest tax of keeping the domain package transport-ignorant, and precisely the
boundary-adapter exemption in R11's falsifying questions. Then, and only then, the
"tempting wrong fix" above becomes the right ceiling: shrink the switch to pure
dispatch (one `fillKafka(&req, p)`-style converter per case, zero inline
field-fiddling) and stop.

Note this rejection is orthogonal to the juiciness rejection in
`anti-if-dispatch.md` Move 3: there the extraction *could* be written but isn't
worth it; here it *cannot* be written where it belongs, at any price.

The decision test, two questions in order:

1. *Why am I switching on type and unpacking fields?* → the behavior wants to live
   on the types (R11).
2. *Does the types' package own this output format?* → yes: interface method, the
   switch dies. No: thin dispatch switch, and the boundary earns its keep.
